author: bigmistqke
message:
experiment(gate): add a way to watch a run already in progress

A full run generates a probe per claim and runs each one, which takes a while,
and there was no way to see how far it had got or what it had found without
waiting for it to finish. But every step leaves its evidence on disk — the
cached probe, the test result, the coverage — so the verdict for any claim that
has finished can be recomputed from those without running anything again.

This reads that evidence and prints the running tally. It is the same verdict
logic the run itself uses, pointed at the artifacts instead of at a live probe,
so watching a run and re-deriving verdicts after a change to that logic are the
same command. Run it against a run in flight and it shows what is decided so far
and what is still pending.

Decision: 1ea16b4a-69ec-4a75-aee5-7c07bfcd35c1

author: bigmistqke
message:
experiment(gate): verify claims by running probes and checking they reached the code

The experiment now runs end to end. For each claim it asks a fresh model for one
probe that fails if the claim is true, runs that probe alone in a pinned copy of
hive under coverage, and reads the result only after checking that the probe
actually executed the lines it said it would.

Two things had to be got right, and the three claims with known answers caught
both. The first was telling a real assertion failure from a probe that threw in
its setup: vitest reports both as a failed test, and it strips an expect()
failure to a bare description while a thrown error keeps its class name, so that
is the seam the classifier reads. The second, and the important one, was what it
means to reach the code. The obvious rule — the probe touched at least one line
it named — passed a probe for a claim about a replay path that is dead under an
in-memory database: the probe named that path and a dozen lines common to every
replay, ran only the common ones, and the claim it was written for was reported
false without its own code ever running. So a probe must now run every statement
line it declares. Naming the buggy path and not reaching it is no longer a
refutation; it is the honest report that the path could not be tested here.

With that, the three known claims land where they should: the real bug confirmed,
and the two that live on the dead path reported unreachable rather than refuted.
The naive version reported both as refuted, which is what makes this a real check
and not a ceremonial one.

Decision: 1ea16b4a-69ec-4a75-aee5-7c07bfcd35c1

author: bigmistqke
message:
experiment(gate): prove a probe's coverage lands on source, not build output

The gate will decide whether a probe touched the lines it claims to, and it does
that by reading coverage. hive's tests import the compiled package rather than
its source, so the coverage could just as well have described the build output,
and then every line number the gate reasons about would point into a file
nobody wrote. So before building anything on top of it, this runs one probe for
a bug already known to be real and looks at where the coverage actually landed.

It landed on the source. The probe failed exactly as it should, since the bug is
real, and the coverage named the source file with hundreds of covered
statements, so line-level reach is available and the design holds as written.

One detail earned its place while proving this: coverage has to be told to
report even when the test fails, because a confirmed finding is precisely a
probe that fails while reaching its code, and the default drops coverage on
failure. Without that flag every real bug would look like unreachable code.

Decision: 1ea16b4a-69ec-4a75-aee5-7c07bfcd35c1

author: bigmistqke
message:
docs(v3): rewrite the handoff around what was actually shown

Replaces the handoff written at the start of the session, whose proposal has
since been abandoned and whose survey of the repository is out of date.

Separates what was demonstrated from what was merely designed, because only one
thing was built. A separate session with no memory of the conversation, given
one prompt and one file, found more than a careful pass made with hours of
context on the same subject. Of the twenty-two problems it reported, one is
confirmed by a failing test and twenty remain unproven, which says the part
worth building is the part that sorts them. Five hand-written tests were
measured and two of them do any work. Three ordinary claims about a clamping
function turn out to contradict each other on an input nobody had thought of.
And two of three checks written to test all this passed while executing nothing
at all, because the code they aimed at is unreachable under the test setup.

It also records four occasions in this session where a tidy story was told ahead
of the evidence and had to be withdrawn, and notes that a person caught every
one of them. That is the same failure the whole design is meant to catch, and it
argues that whatever does the catching had better not be another model.

Ranks what to do next, lists the confirmed problems found in the two neighbouring
projects and left unfixed, and keeps the objections that were never answered:
nobody has shown the review will actually happen, a decision never made cannot be
detected, know-how has nowhere to live, and passing every check means coherent,
never wise.

Decision: 08888b2f-73ff-44c9-b5e5-3d2fb8869fb8
Implements: 1451a700-644a-4f6a-9615-716f7c76d3a6

author: bigmistqke
message:
docs(v3): correct the claim that the model can fetch what it needs

Yesterday's commit concluded that a model given a starting point will go and
find everything it needs, and used that to delete the component whose job was
to put the decision graph in front of it. The first half of that is right and
the second half is wrong, and the wrong half contradicts the reason this
project exists.

The cold session followed imports and call sites into four other files. That
works because code retrieval is self-guiding: an import says what to read
next, a call site points at a definition, and the structure carries you along.
So code does not need to be rendered into the model's context. It can go and
get it.

Intent cannot be gone and got. The file it was given had no record of what
anyone had decided, so the session reconstructed the mechanism by reading the
source, which is precisely the backwards derivation this project is meant to
abolish. Concluding "let it go and look" does not simplify the idea, it
abandons it.

The run is its own evidence. It produced twenty-two unspecified cases and
could not rank one of them. It had no way to tell a broken promise from a
deliberate postponement, because it had nothing to compare the code against.
That is why a person had to sort the list by hand and why only one item
survived. Knowing what was decided is not decoration on top of the findings.
It is what sorts them.

So the deletion stands for code and is reversed for intent, in a smaller
shape. The graph does not need to be summarised, zoomed, or squeezed into a
prompt. It needs one link, from a region of code to the decisions that
constrain it, so that a model reading a file can ask what was decided about it
and walk there the same way it walks from an import to a definition. You
cannot search for a decision you do not know exists; the link is what makes it
findable.

author: bigmistqke
message:
docs(v3): record the blind test, and cut the rendering layer it disproved

The design assumed a model could be asked to break a module into checkable
claims and would produce claims with teeth, rather than restatements of the
happy path. Nothing had tested that, and nothing else in the design mattered
if it were false. This records the test.

A separate headless session, with no memory of the design conversation, was
given one prompt and one file: the event store of the decision-tracking tool
this project uses. It returned twenty-nine claims, fourteen unspecified
cases, and eight contradictions. An independent pass done by hand, written
down and sealed beforehand, found eight things; the cold session found seven
of them, several more besides, and usually put them better.

One of its findings is confirmed by a failing test. Recording a change to a
node's confidence and then rebuilding the database from the log turns that
change into a change of the node's status, because the commit subject line
is hardcoded to say status. The node's status becomes the string "95".

The sealed prediction was that a session given a single file would miss
everything that spans files. That was wrong, and the reason it was wrong
removes a whole component from the design. The session read four other files
on its own initiative, and its best findings came from doing so. You do not
have to render the graph into the model's context. You give it a starting
point and let it go and look. The fisheye views, the code-shaped
serialisation and the cached summaries are all deleted.

The more useful lesson is about the gate rather than the engine. Twenty-two
claims went in and one came out confirmed, one traced to its exact lines,
and twenty unproven. Two of the three probe tests written to check the claims
passed while testing nothing at all: the tool's own test database lives in
memory, so a file existence check it branches on is always false, so every
one of its one hundred and sixty-two tests takes one path and the other path
has never once been executed. The suite is green and the code is unreached.
A model that produces twenty-two plausible claims and no way to sort them is
a liability. The thing worth building is what sorts them.

Adds the prompt, the raw output, the sealed hand pass and the probe tests, so
the run can be re-read and re-run.

author: bigmistqke
message:
docs(v3): add the design for deriving tests from decomposed decisions

Adds a new package directory holding a design document and the two
experiments that back it.

The design proposes that an architectural decision should not be a block
of prose. It should be broken into individual claims, each carrying a
predicate over its inputs, the answer it promises, and a record of how it
is checked: by the type system, by a test, by human review, or not at all.
Claims can nest, and a test is derived for each leaf. Three checks then
become mechanical rather than a matter of taste: inputs no claim speaks to,
inputs two claims answer differently, and tests that catch nothing another
test already catches.

The reason for all this is that asking a language model to "write tests for
X" is an unbounded request, so it fills the space with plausible but
redundant tests. The two scripts in the experiments directory measure that
claim rather than assert it.

The first script breaks the max example's dataflow graph in seven ways,
compiles each one through the existing compiler into WebAssembly, and runs
the five hand-written tests against every version. Only two of the five
catch anything the other tests miss. One of them cannot fail at all: when
both inputs are equal, any implementation that returns either input passes.

The second script takes the three claims an author would naturally write
for a clamp function and looks for inputs that no claim covers and inputs
that two claims answer differently. It finds ten contradictions, every one
of them a case where the minimum exceeds the maximum. Nobody had to know
that edge case in advance for the check to surface it.

The handoff note is kept for the survey of the existing packages it
contains, but its own proposal is marked superseded by the design.

message:
feat(v2): add full gradient experiment with calculator example

v2 explores the full gradient from vision to AST:
- Vision/Architecture/Component/Function layers have descriptions (intent)
- Dataflow layer is flat DAG with explicit wiring and shared nodes
- AST layer is nested tree structure, code generated from it

Key insight: dataflow shows data dependencies, AST shows syntactic
structure. Function layer is the boundary between described intent
and structural implementation.

Also adds READMEs documenting v1 (structural skeleton) and v2 (full gradient).
